system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2186-02-20 14:21:00 to 2186-02-22 12:05:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and hypogammaglobulinemia was admitted for a scheduled IVIG infusion using Privigen, a low osmolar agent, due to prior adverse reactions with other formulations. During the infusion, he developed hypertension with systolic pressure up to 200 and transient chest tightness, which was distinct from his usual anginal symptoms and not associated with EKG changes. He also experienced dizziness and a delayed episode of chest tightness and shortness of breath, which resolved without intervention. His blood pressure was managed by slowing the infusion rate, and no medication changes were made. His mitochondrial myopathy and cardiac conditions remained stable. Mild acidosis and dehydration improved with supportive care. He was discharged home in stable condition with instructions to follow up on blood pressure and discuss infusion tolerance with his allergist.
problems: Coronary atherosclerosis of native coronary artery
Unspecified disorder of kidney and ureter

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I’m Dr. ___. You’re here today for your scheduled IVIG infusion, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. This is my fourth one. But I’ve been getting them in the hospital because of reactions I’ve had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see from your history. You’ve had some chest tightness and high blood pressure after past infusions. We’ll monitor you closely today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I actually had some sweating and squeezing chest pain this morning—about a 4 out of 10. Felt faint and nauseous too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you said it’s similar to how you feel when you’re dehydrated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. I get that a lot because of my mitochondrial disease. But I wanted to mention it just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. We’ll keep an eye on your vitals. We’re going to start you on a saline infusion first—1900cc over several hours—to help with fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s what I usually get at home. Every week or so, I get IV fluids for my orthostatic hypotension.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and it’s especially important today before the IVIG. We want to minimize any side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Oh, and I’ve been meaning to mention—I’ve got this rash on my left lower leg. It’s been growing for about a month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let me take a look.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see a red, slightly raised patch with scaling. It’s well-defined but irregular. You said it’s itchy and crusts over?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes. It feels like the squamous cell carcinoma I had removed a few years ago. I also have these tumors in my thigh I see the orthopedic oncologist for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, we should have your dermatologist evaluate this. It may be eczema, but we don’t want to miss anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. I’ll make sure to bring it up at my next appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your saline infusion is halfway done. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit better. The chest tightness has eased. Still a little lightheaded when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected with your autonomic dysfunction. We’ll keep monitoring. We’ll finish the fluids tonight and give IVIG tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re going to prep for your IVIG today. First, we’ll check your labs, including your IgG levels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are those the immune protein levels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your IgG subclasses 1 and 3 are a bit low, which confirms you still need the IVIG. We’ll give you 15 grams today—half your usual dose, but more frequently now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, switching to every two weeks instead of monthly. I hope that helps with side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. We’ll also pre-medicate you with Benadryl and Tylenol to reduce reaction risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting the IVIG now. We’ll go slowly and check your vitals every 15 minutes at first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doc, I’m starting to feel that chest tightness again. And short of breath. A little nauseous too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, let’s slow the infusion. We’ll get an EKG and check your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your EKG looks stable—no signs of heart strain. Blood pressure is 151/96, a bit high but not alarming. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is this dangerous? Could it be my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your troponin levels—those are heart damage markers—and they’re normal. This seems like a reaction to the IVIG, not a heart issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Like what I’ve had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very similar. We’ll continue at a slower rate and watch you closely. The symptoms should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. The chest tightness has eased, and your breathing is normal. We finished the IVIG.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel more like myself. Still a mild headache, but nothing like earlier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. We’ll keep you overnight for observation, as usual, and plan to discharge tomorrow if you stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs are normal. Troponins stayed negative, and your blood count is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No more chest pain or nausea. Headache’s gone too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your physical exam is also improved—abdomen is no longer tender, and your skin lesion looks unchanged.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We recommend you follow up with your dermatologist about that leg rash, given your history of skin cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my IVIG schedule—every two weeks—is still on track?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And no changes to your other medications. You’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Thanks for watching me so closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. If you develop severe headache, chest pain, or trouble breathing at home, go to the ER. Otherwise, keep your follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll call my team if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well with the IVIG overall—more strength, you said?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I feel stronger than before I started. Worth the side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. We’ll keep supporting you through these infusions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll see you in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___. Safe travels home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of mitochondrial myopathy, coronary artery disease, and hypogammaglobulinemia was admitted for a scheduled IVIG infusion, now adjusted to a half-dose every two weeks. Upon admission, he reported baseline symptoms of chest tightness, diaphoresis, nausea, and lightheadedness, which he associates with dehydration due to autonomic dysfunction. He received a 1900cc saline infusion overnight to optimize fluid status. The next day, he was pre-medicated and received 15g of IVIG, after which he developed transient chest tightness, shortness of breath, nausea, and headache—consistent with prior infusion reactions. Serial troponins and EKGs showed no evidence of cardiac ischemia. Symptoms resolved by the following morning. A chronic skin lesion on the left lower extremity, growing over the past month and reminiscent of prior squamous cell carcinoma, was noted, and dermatology follow-up was recommended. The patient remained stable, and no medication changes were made. He was discharged home in good condition with plans to continue outpatient IVIG and follow-up with specialists.
